soil-env-335.title: How soil keeps cycling nutrients and organic matter
soil-env-335.text:
The nutrients in soil particles start out locked in crystals. Soil water carrying carbon dioxide slowly dissolves them, a process called {{ref:soil-found-058}}, and releases them into the soil solution, the water held among the particles.

Plants then take over. They capture carbon by photosynthesis, absorb water and nutrients, and store both in biomass. When plants die or are eaten, organisms decompose the residues and manure, and the nutrients become available again. This loop is the {{ref:soil-fert-146}}.

Soil also keeps a reserve. Clays bond with organic molecules, and aggregates shield particles from decomposers. The result is a store of nutrients and energy, richest in the deep-rooted soils of prairie and steppe.

Plowing broke the loop. It sped decomposition, so more {{ref:soil-found-045}} was lost than returned, and nutrients left with the crop. Fertilizers later replaced the nutrients, but replacing the lost carbon was mostly ignored. That matters because organic matter forms aggregates that give water storage and gas exchange. Mineral particles and pores give a soil its structure, yet organic matter mostly makes it fertile.

soil-env-349.title: What a soil health assessment can tell a farmer
soil-env-349.text:
A soil health assessment answers a practical question: what is wrong with this soil, and is it getting better? It can target problems such as phosphorus deficiency or surface compaction. Over several years it can show whether cover crops, a new rotation or reduced tillage are improving the soil.

It also bears on value. Well-managed healthy soil should be worth more when sold or rented, since it produces more with fewer purchased inputs. That gives owners a reason to invest in it.

Assessment works at three levels of detail: general field observations, field assessments using qualitative indicators, and quantitative soil health tests. All of them build on {{ref:soil-env-174}}.

soil-env-350.title: Reading soil health in the field
soil-env-350.text:
A spade, a few minutes and a careful eye can reveal a lot about a field. Field indicators are observations of cover, crusting, ponding, aggregates, hardness, color, roots and organisms, and they point to a soil's key limitations. The NRCS Cropland In-Field Soil Health Assessment Worksheet rates soil cover, residue breakdown, surface crusts, ponding, penetration resistance, water-stable aggregates, structure, color, roots, biological diversity and biopores. It is one way to carry out a {{ref:soil-env-349}}.

Timing matters. Soil health is best measured in early spring and late fall, when the soil is moist. Measurements vary with moisture and season: a hard soil after a dry spring may be soft after a wet one, and earthworms go deeper in dry spells. So sample at least 10 spots and avoid headlands. Problems such as runoff or drought stress show better in wet or dry periods.

Absence of a sign proves little. Crusting, ponding, slaked patches downslope and rills or gullies signal poor aggregate stability, runoff and erosion, but they appear only after hard rain.

Color reflects mineralogy, oxidation and organic matter. Within one soil type darker generally means better, though adding organic matter may take years to change color.

soil-env-333.title: Building a degraded soil back into a healthy one
soil-env-333.text:
Some soil problems take an afternoon to fix. Liming an acid soil is one. Others are close to permanent: a shallow soil can hardly be deepened, and a clay subsoil that causes poor drainage needs tile drainage at significant economic and environmental cost.

Building soil means turning a degraded or low-quality soil into a high-quality one through understanding and sustained action that mirrors how plants and organic matter build soil in nature. {{ref:soil-found-045}} benefits almost all healthy-soil characteristics, even pest management. Managing it is therefore the foundation, along with limiting compaction and managing nutrients.

General approaches are to minimize {{ref:soil-agri-095}} and other disturbance, add diverse organic materials, and keep live roots in the ground through rotations and a {{ref:soil-agri-066}} with varied root systems. Further steps are to keep the soil covered with cover crops or residue against rain and temperature extremes, manage traffic to protect structure, and manage pH and nutrients without polluting water. In arid regions the sodium or salt in the soil should also be reduced.

soil-env-336.title: How farming wears soil out in a downward spiral
soil-env-336.text:
Cultivated soil rarely fails all at once. {{ref:soil-agri-095}} breaks aggregates, and organic matter is lost faster. Soils with lower organic matter and weaker aggregation erode faster, and {{ref:soil-water-001}} removes the organic-rich topsoil. That starts a downward spiral of compaction, poor infiltration and root growth, and nutrient decline. In arid regions, irrigation adds another path: it can make soils saline, so salts in the water must be leached beneath the root zone.

The speed depends on the soil. Tropical rainforest soils can degrade within two or three years of conversion to cropland, which is why slash-and-burn developed. Great Plains soils took many decades to show degradation.

The scale is large. Degradation has cut yields on about 20% of the world's cropland and 19-27% of grasslands and rangelands, and most agricultural soils are in fair, poor or very poor condition. Some 30-40 billion tons of topsoil are eroded from the world's croplands each year.

History shows the cost. Rapid soil degradation in the temperate forests of the eastern United States pushed agriculture westward. Elsewhere the lost productivity led either to colonial ventures to feed the citizenry, like the Romans invading the Egyptian breadbasket, or to the decline of the civilization. Fertility lasted for centuries only in convergence zones such as valleys and deltas, where nutrients and sediments flow together.

soil-env-337.title: From soil to plant to person: the health chain
soil-env-337.text:
Soil reaches people by more than one route. It affects them directly: dust storms from bare soils can cause respiratory problems and lung damage, while frequent early contact with soil and farm animals is linked to fewer allergies and a stronger immune system.

The longer route runs through plants. Crops remove nutrients that natural systems recycle. Synthetic fertilizers mostly replace nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium and calcium but not trace minerals, especially where farmers apply standard blends without soil analysis. Some soils are naturally low in elements such as selenium, which affects animals and humans more than plants. Others become toxic through pollution, cadmium-rich fertilizers or Bangladesh tube-well irrigation that put arsenic into rice.

The largest effect of degradation is lost capacity to produce enough nutritious food, especially for rural families in developing countries who eat from their own farms. Mineral deficiency is rare in developed societies because diets come from many regions. Proving soil-health effects on human health is hard, because of dietary complexity and ethical limits on trials. The chain starts with {{ref:soil-env-174}}.

soil-env-365.title: Keeping living roots in the ground all year
soil-env-365.text:
Natural forests and prairies are never bare. They keep a continuous plant cover and a litter layer, whereas annual crops leave periods with no living plants, and prairie fallow was shown early on to lower soil organic matter. The practice of continuous living plants tries to close those gaps, mainly by perennializing cropping systems, and it protects soil, diversifies systems and builds soil carbon.

The root system explains much of the gain. Plants allocate roughly 40% of net photosynthetic carbon to roots, and perennials give more carbon input than annuals because of larger root systems and a longer photosynthesis period. Roots and their microbial communities improve aggregation and hydraulic conductivity. In dry regions they raise porosity and the water retained at field capacity. Longer growth and transpiration from deep in the profile also help reduce salinity, because cover and roots limit evaporation and upward salt movement.

Annual systems can approximate it with winter annuals such as winter wheat or fall rye, fall and spring cover crops, relay cropping or intercropping, perennial forages and agroforestry. A {{ref:soil-agri-066}} is the simplest step.

soil-env-352.title: Laboratory tests that measure how alive a soil is
soil-env-352.text:
For years the standard soil test was chemical, and that gave a chemical bias that favored quick-fix fertilizer use. Laboratory soil health tests add biological and physical indicators to the chemical ones, to assess the soil processes that support ecosystem services. As of 2020 no single standard soil health test exists, though all agree it needs biological, physical and chemical indicators and interpretation by climate and texture. This is the quantitative end of {{ref:soil-env-177}}.

Aggregate stability reflects infiltration, crusting and tilth and responds fast to reduced tillage, cover crops or manure. Available water capacity depends more on texture than on management. Soil organic matter is often the single most important indicator but changes too slowly. Active carbon, oxidized by potassium permanganate, responds quickly, and soil protein does too, especially with more legumes. Soil respiration integrates microbial abundance and activity and tracks nitrogen mineralization potential. The bean root rot bioassay gauges root health and disease pressure from nematodes and fungi such as Fusarium, Pythium and Rhizoctonia.

Context adds tests. Salts and sodium should be tested in arid regions and greenhouses, and heavy metals, radioactive materials, solvents and petroleum products in urban or industrial soils.

soil-env-364.title: The six Cs: practices that build soil health
soil-env-364.text:
The six practices all start with C, to stress the role of carbon in soil health. They are compaction reduction, conservation tillage, continuous living plants, cover crops, crop and animal diversity, and composts and amendments. Together they protect the soil against threats, diversify or perennialize annual cropping, and build soil carbon.

The threats they address are erosion, compaction, organic matter decline, nutrient depletion or excess, biodiversity loss, salinization, desertification and contamination. The practices can be used singly or combined, and in combination they interact in varying ways. At a long-term Ontario site, soil health scores rose as more of them were adopted. Each rests on {{ref:soil-env-174}}.

soil-env-340.title: What undisturbed ecosystems teach about farming
soil-env-340.text:
A prairie or forest left alone recovers from fire, wind or excess rain. Undisturbed natural systems are stable and rebound quickly, and their traits give a model for farming.

They use energy efficiently through food webs, capture and use rainfall, and cycle nutrients, which keeps the ecosystem from running down and protects water quality. Rain enters porous soil instead of running off, recharging groundwater and releasing water slowly to streams. High aboveground and soil biodiversity, in the sense of {{ref:soil-bio-008}}, supplies nutrients and checks disease. Competition and antagonisms such as antibiotics keep soilborne pathogens from causing disease in natural grassland or forest.

Efficiency and diversity make these systems nearly self-sufficient, needing only sunlight and rain. Crop production disturbs them to favor one or a few species.

soil-env-341.title: Growing healthy crops by preventing problems
soil-env-341.text:
Spraying and fumigating react to trouble after it starts. Ecological management is proactive and preventive: it grows healthy plants with strong defenses, suppresses pests and enhances beneficial organisms by improving habitat both aboveground and in the soil. Routine soil fumigation or broad-spectrum herbicides create dependency on purchased inputs, weaken resilience and promote resistance. The model is the {{ref:soil-env-340}}.

Aboveground practices include resistant varieties, suitable planting density, variety blends, perimeter trap crops and flowering strips for beneficial insects. In the soil, the aim is to minimize disturbance and compaction, keep soil covered with residue, perennial forages and cover crops, maximize biodiversity, manage water, and keep pH and nutrients in range by routine testing.

A vigorous winter legume cover crop, such as crimson clover in the southern US or hairy vetch in the north, can supply all the nitrogen for the next crop. Complex rotations with different plant families, and sod crops left undisturbed for years, are central. Tillage buries residue and breaks aggregates, leaving soil prone to erosion.

soil-env-330.title: A quick field test for soil nitrate
soil-env-330.text:
A color strip can estimate nitrate in minutes. Shake a soil subsample 1:1 by volume with distilled water, filter it, put drops on a strip and read the color change after 60 seconds. The result estimates nitrate-N in ppm, the product of {{ref:soil-fert-112}}. Nitrite rarely occurs in measurable amounts in soil, so the nitrite pad reading is not recorded.

The strip reads at most 50 ppm. A sample at the limit is diluted with equal drops of water and the reading multiplied by 2, or by 4 if diluted again. Pounds of nitrate-N per acre follow from ppm, sampling depth and {{ref:soil-phys-060}}, which can be assumed to be 1.1 g/cm3 for garden topsoil and 1.5 g/cm3 for subsoil.

soil-env-355.title: Why soil health practices work best together
soil-env-355.text:
Each soil health practice affects the others, so they work best combined and matched to the needs and opportunities of the farm. Practices that improve soil health generally also improve farm economics through higher, steadier yields and lower inputs. The return may take a few years, though, and may need equipment such as new tillage tools and planters.

Big changes suit strategic moments, such as a new planter or good prices. Before planting an orchard, vineyard or landscape, or switching to no-till, add organic matter, relieve subsoil compaction and correct nutrient deficiencies. Managing {{ref:soil-env-174}} is a long-term commitment with no silver bullets, and it needs integration of physical, biological and chemical processes.

soil-env-358.title: Preventing soil problems before they appear
soil-env-358.text:
Holistic soil health management aims to prevent problems, as preventive medicine does, and diagnoses them by observation and testing. What suits an operation depends on soils, climate, enterprise, region, markets and goals. Tests from {{ref:soil-env-177}} guide the targeting of constraints but rarely give a simple recipe.

The advice is to test each field every two to three years, preferably with comprehensive soil health analyses, and to add amendments only when needed. Keeping test records lets changes be followed over the years and practices fine-tuned.

soil-env-344.title: How attacked plants call for help
soil-env-344.text:
A plant under attack is not silent. Damaged plants produce extra-floral nectar that feeds beneficials, and airborne volatiles that guide small wasps to a caterpillar host, in which the wasp lays eggs that kill it.

The signal can run underground, through the {{ref:soil-bio-143}}. Roots of some corn varieties attacked by western corn rootworm release a chemical that attracts a nematode killing the larvae. Breeding lost this trait in US corn, but wild relatives and European varieties retain it. Neighboring plants can even sense chemicals from wounded leaves and start making defenses before being attacked.

soil-env-357.title: Protecting soil organic matter with less tillage
soil-env-357.text:
Leaving residue on the surface makes it easier to hold on to organic matter. Less disturbance keeps biological activity and decomposition near the surface, and keeps a structure that lets rain infiltrate quickly. Surface residue or mulch encourages earthworms, keeps soil moist and moderates temperature extremes.

Minimum tillage greatly reduces erosion compared with conventional tillage, and contour tillage, contour strip cropping and terracing also help keep organic matter. There is a catch: heavy surface residue can harbor insects and disease organisms, so rotation matters even more. Problems can be worse in {{ref:soil-agri-117}} monoculture.

soil-env-356.title: Keeping a balance sheet for soil health
soil-env-356.text:
Think of soil health as a bank account. Practices that build it are credits, and practices that degrade it are debits. Credits include manure additions, reduced tillage and cover crops. Debits include compaction from field traffic and intensive tillage.

Farming systems differ in their balance sheet: daily harvesting forces traffic on wet soil, and small-seeded crops need intensive tillage in the row. An unavoidable bad practice should be balanced with a good one, or its impact reduced, for example by confining traffic to certain lanes. The account is kept in terms of {{ref:soil-env-174}}.

soil-env-359.title: Quick fixes and lasting fixes for soil constraints
soil-env-359.text:
Management guidelines for soil constraints come in two kinds. Short-term or intermittent responses give quick results and may need repeating. Long-term approaches give no quick fix but address the concern more sustainably. The same practices are often recommended for different constraints because they address several concerns at once.

For low aggregate stability the short-term fix is fresh organic materials and the long-term fix is reduced tillage, surface mulch and sod rotation. For low available water capacity it is stable organic materials such as compost, lignin-rich residues and biochar. Recommendations for physical and biological constraints are less precise than for nutrients, because those systems are more complex and the research base is weaker. The constraints themselves come from {{ref:soil-env-177}}.
